To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the protein patterns of gingival tissue and plasma are altered by inflammation and that the protein patterns for tissue and plasma are not identical.

1) the electrophoretic protein patterns of gingiva are significantly different from the protein patterns of blood plasma and 2) the protein patterns of clinically inflamed gingiva are different from the protein pattern of clinically normal gingiva.
the protein patterns of gingival tissue and gingival blood differ from those of the normal venous blood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the comparative analysis of normal and inflamed gingival tissue, and of gingival blood.
the development of an analytical technique to study the biochemical changes in the gingiva which occur during the development of periodontitis.

the development of a method of protein separation that will permit identification of the specific protein differences that exist between the gingival fluid from clinically normal and inflamned tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no consistent differences in the protein patterns between normal and inflamed gingiva.
the protein patterns of the gingival tissue and blood are different.
the electrophoretic patterns of gingival homogenate supernatants are not the same as those of blood plasma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the anionic and cations disc electrophoretic protein patterns of the inflamed tissue were different from those of the normal tissue, and that the anionic disc electrophoretograms for the plasma and venous blood samples were similar, whereas the cationic patterns of the plasma and venious blood samples were different.
the protein pattern differences between clinically normal and clinically diseased gingiva are more pronounced when the tissue is separated on a cationic disc.

there is a marked qualitative difference in the protein patterns of the gingiva and blood, and that there is a significant qualitative difference in the patterns of the normal and inflamed gingival tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have demonstrated the potential of this approach to identify novel biomarkers for gingival inflammation, and that we have demonstrated that the approach is robust, reproducible, and sensitive to the presence of gingival inflammation.
the anionic and cations gel electrophoreses are useful for detecting protein changes in gingival tissues and plasma.
the inflammatory response is a very complex and dynamic process that is not limited to the release of cytokines and other mediators.
